solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Long heart-to-heart with your local solicitor?

parts.note: L is a standard abbreviation for long, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: read as 'the heart of the following word', this takes the single central letter of the word heart

parts.note: yer is the colloquial, local-dialect form of the word your

explanation.surface: A lengthy confidential chat with the neighbourhood legal adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'heart-to-heart' looks like one idiom for a frank talk, but it splits: 'heart-to' points at the middle of the second 'heart', its central A.
explanation.definitionFit: A solicitor in Britain is a kind of legal practitioner, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Desperate pal's stag do

indicators.note: a do is a party, but read as a verb it tells the solver to work these letters into a new arrangement

parts.note: the possessive s counts here as a letter of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A friend's bachelor party has become a frantic affair.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag do is a British bachelor party; 'do' is the anagram signal working on PALSSTAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-gasp effort is a final frantic one, made in desperation at the very end.

clue.text: Mystery of Welsh bricklaying gang

parts.note: a hod is the trough a labourer uses to carry bricks, so it stands for bricklaying
a gang is a group or team, a unit

explanation.surface: A puzzling tale about a crew of builders from Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime novel built around solving a puzzle is called by this informal name, a detective mystery.

clue.text: Perhaps female shuns bravery for self-interest

parts.note: eg, for example, signals an instance, as perhaps does

indicators.note: to shun something is to avoid it, so these letters are removed

parts.note: heroism is great bravery
her is a female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman turns her back on courage in favour of looking after herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps female' looks like one phrase, but 'Perhaps' gives EG and 'female' is HER, taken out of HEROISM to leave OISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Egoism is a philosophy of acting chiefly for one's own advantage, putting oneself first.

clue.text: Prince excluded from redevelopment of specified buildings

indicators.note: being shut out of a group means these letters are left out of the pool
redeveloping a site rebuilds it, so the letters are rebuilt in new order

explanation.surface: A royal is left out of a plan to rebuild particular properties.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P from SPECIFIED and rearrange the remaining eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice is a large, imposing building, so the plural matches buildings.

clue.text: Idiots sans eyes, we hear …

indicators.note: eyes said aloud is the letter name I twice, and sans means without, so both I's are removed

explanation.surface: Fools without their eyes, so people say, trail off into silence.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the punctuation itself: the ellipsis at the end of the clue is a row of small points.
explanation.definitionFit: An ellipsis is printed as three small points, so the clue's trailing mark is literally what it describes.

clue.text: Notorious old lady in uniform

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, as the old lady is placed in the uniform

parts.note: uniform means even and unvarying, or flat
gran is a grandmother, an old lady

explanation.surface: An infamous elderly woman is seen dressed in uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like clothing, but here it is the adjective meaning even, FLAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagrant means glaringly obvious and shocking, as with notorious, conspicuous wrongdoing.

clue.text: Play has to happen over 24 hours, answer goes

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed over another comes before it in the grid

parts.note: to come about is to happen, so come stands for it

indicators.note: something that goes departs, so this letter is dropped

parts.note: a day is twenty-four hours

explanation.surface: A drama must take place within a single day, but without its resolution.
explanation.walkthrough: Classical drama's unity of time had a play's action happen within a day, which the surface borrows.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedy is a type of stage play, a light-hearted one with a happy ending.

clue.text: She has sex with many, but not with choirboy?

indicators.note: but not names a thing excluded, so this letter is taken away

parts.note: a swinger is a person who has many sexual partners

explanation.surface: A promiscuous woman is contrasted with an innocent young chorister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' does double duty in the surface but in the parse it is the W removed from SWINGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A choirboy is a young male who performs vocal music in a church choir, an example of a vocalist.

clue.text: Ban on circuses, in retrospect, is absolutely right

indicators.note: looking back means the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: no, as in 'no smoking', is a ban on something
big tops are circus tents, so tops stands for circuses

explanation.surface: A prohibition on travelling circuses is seen, looking back, to have been justified.
explanation.walkthrough: NO TOPS read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spot on hits the exact point, so it is completely correct.

clue.text: Smart New Labour shams

indicators.note: to labour material is to work it over, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political jibe that the slick New Labour project was all front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Labour' looks like the 1990s party brand; 'New' is fodder and 'Labour' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw man is a sham argument or front, set up only to be knocked down.

clue.text: Implicate yours truly over manipulation of Libor

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the letters of this short word are reversed

parts.note: yours truly is a jocular way of saying me

indicators.note: manipulating these letters moves them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to involvement in the rigging of a banking interest rate.
explanation.walkthrough: LIBOR is the London interbank lending rate, famously rigged by bank traders around 2012.
explanation.definitionFit: To embroil someone is to drag them into a conflict, involving or implicating them.

clue.text: Voice became a little repulsive

indicators.note: to voice words is to say them aloud, so the clue gives how this sounds

parts.note: grew some means increased a little, became somewhat more

explanation.surface: A singer's voice turned somewhat unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Gruesome means horrible to look at, causing revulsion.

clue.text: Doctor's keenness to clear bed

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor; the 's joins it to the next piece
edge is sharpness or keenness, as in an edge to one's appetite

explanation.surface: A physician is eager to free up a hospital bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bed' is a riverbed or seabed, not a hospital one.
explanation.definitionFit: Dredging scoops mud and silt from the bottom of a river or harbour to clear it.

clue.text: Spurs turned up without energy or staying power

indicators.note: without means lacking, so this letter is taken away
in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: to spur is to stir into action or animate
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Tottenham Hotspur, coming up short of energy, lacked endurance.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur football club, but here it is a verb. ANIMATES reversed gives SETAMINA; losing an E leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the physical endurance to keep going, the power of staying the course.

clue.text: Asking, like Andersen's emperor, for coat

indicators.note: the emperor in Andersen's tale went out naked, so the word is stripped of its outer letters

explanation.surface: A request, in the manner of the emperor in the fairy tale, for something to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hans Christian Andersen's 'The Emperor's New Clothes' the emperor parades naked; a 'naked' word loses its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin is the natural outer covering of an animal, its coat or pelt.

clue.text: Dictator's correcting text

indicators.note: a dictator here is one who dictates words aloud, so the clue gives a sound

parts.note: righting a wrong is correcting it

explanation.surface: A tyrant is revising what has been written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' looks like a tyrant, but it is someone dictating speech, which signals a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing as a noun is written words, a body of text.

clue.text: One in a hundred supports fund for the drinking of alcohol

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that supports another sits below it

parts.note: a pot is a pool of money, a fund
taken as written

indicators.note: one letter goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: a ton is slang for a hundred
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: One per cent of the money backs a scheme to pay for booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in a hundred' looks like a percentage; it is the Roman one placed inside the slang hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: A potation is an old-fashioned word for a drink or the act of drinking, especially of liquor.

clue.text: Blokes curse Y-fronts, among other things

parts.note: blokes is British slang for men
to curse is to swear

explanation.surface: Men complain about their briefs.
explanation.walkthrough: Y-fronts are British men's briefs with an upside-down Y-shaped front.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing for males includes underpants such as these, so the definition is by example.

clue.text: Cock bird getting closer to mate in springtime

indicators.note: the bird and letter are set inside the spring month

parts.note: May is a month of springtime
a lark is a songbird

indicators.note: the closer of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A male bird gets close to its partner in the breeding season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cock' looks like a rooster, but it is the British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock in British slang means rubbish or nonsense talk, as in 'a load of cock'.

clue.text: The end of romance is accepted by most women, alas

indicators.note: something accepted by another is taken in, placed inside it
most of a word is all but its last letter
the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Most women take in a fading love affair, sighing at its close.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an archaic exclamation of sorrow or lament, like alas.

clue.text: Smashing a treasure from the east

indicators.note: read from the east, an across entry runs right to left, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a gem is something treasured, a precious stone

explanation.surface: A precious find arrives from the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: Mega is informal slang for excellent or terrific, as smashing is.

clue.text: Silence a bunch of pigs, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as said aloud, so the clue gives a sound

parts.note: a sty-full is as many pigs as fill a sty

explanation.surface: Quiet a noisy group of swine, so people say.
explanation.definitionFit: To stifle a sound is to suppress or muffle it, bringing quiet.

clue.text: For headless chicken time is over

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that is over another is written above it
losing its head means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a chicken is slang for a coward

explanation.surface: A panicking bird has run out of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headless chicken' looks like the idiom for frantic panic, but 'headless' trims COWARD to OWARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Toward means in the direction of or with a view to, as for does in 'heading for'.

clue.text: Fervently ask individual to get lost

parts.note: to beg is to ask earnestly
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: Earnestly plead with someone to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Begone is an old command to leave at once, like the slang get lost.

clue.text: How amazing to stand in river flowing in both directions!

indicators.note: to stand in a river is to be inside it, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: the Tay is the longest river in Scotland
wow is an exclamation of amazement

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at wading into a current running both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-way traffic moves in both directions, as a two-way street permits.

clue.text: Endures a tour in submarine

indicators.note: a tour goes round about, so the letters are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sits out a long trip aboard a submarine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Submarine' looks like a noun, the vessel, but it is the adjective meaning beneath the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Submarine as an adjective means existing or happening below the surface of the ocean.

clue.text: Monster conger-eel regularly escaping

indicators.note: letters escaping at regular intervals means every other one is dropped

explanation.surface: A huge fish gets away at intervals.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, a monster.

clue.text: Exotic bird flipping over

parts.note: flaming and flipping are both mild British intensifiers, as in 'flipping cheek'
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A rare bird does a somersault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like turning over, but it is the mild British curse word.
explanation.definitionFit: The flamingo is a tropical wading bird with pink plumage, so it counts as an exotic one.

clue.text: Blow kiss for Russian copper

parts.note: KO is a knockout, a decisive blow
a peck is a quick kiss

explanation.surface: A punch and a kiss for a Moscow police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is a low-value coin; a kopeck is a hundredth of a rouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A kopeck is a small Russian coin, and copper is British slang for low-value change.

clue.text: Threaten to kill bug

parts.note: to end something is to finish or kill it
to bug someone is to annoy or anger them

explanation.surface: Someone menaces to exterminate an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger is to put at risk, to threaten the safety of something.

clue.text: Peer into yards on a regular basis

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other

parts.note: Y is an abbreviation for yard, doubled for the plural
an earl is a British peer of the realm

explanation.surface: A nobleman looks closely into gardens at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a verb meaning to look closely; it is the nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done each year happens at regular annual intervals.
